title: Antonelli rues pole slipping away in ‘intense’ Qualifying
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has admitted that he was pleased with his effort in Spanish Grand Prix Qualifying before McLaren’s Lando Norris pipped him to pole position, with the Mercedes driver concluding that it was a “very intense” session at the Madring.

Fresh from his historic victory at the Italian Grand Prix, it looked as though Antonelli would be in front once again as he mingled around the top of the timesheets throughout Qualifying and consistently improved his laps.

His last lap in Q3 was enough to deny Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton pole, but in the final seconds, Norris completed what he labelled “one of the best laps” of his career to snatch P1 by margin of 0.011s over the 20-year-old.

Speaking straight afterwards, Antonelli said of his attempt: “I thought it was a good lap, but then this guy just snatched it away, so a good job to them.

“On my side, a very intense Qualifying – difficult to get the balance right with the track being so hot, but yeah, the lap was pretty clean.

“Obviously it's not easy to put the things together on a track like this, which is quite tricky, but overall I think we did a good job and now we'll try to see what we can do tomorrow.”

The Italian will be hoping to find a way past Norris and add an eighth win to his tally in the Spanish Grand Prix, but many teams have predicted that overtaking will be a significant challenge due to the circuit’s complex layout and lack of long straights.

A strong result would provide a further boost to Antonelli’s title ambitions – he currently holds a 66-point advantage over his nearest rival and team mate George Russell, who could only manage P6 in Qualifying.

Asked what his plan is for the race, Antonelli replied: “Hopefully a good start. Hopefully we can get the jump. If the opportunity comes to win the race, we’ll try to take it.

“Otherwise, we’ll just try to do our best race and then we’ll see what happens.”

title: Sainz hit with grid penalty for Spanish GP
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has been handed a grid penalty for the Spanish Grand Prix after a Qualifying infringement.

The Williams driver was found to have impeded Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac during Saturday's Qualifying session through Turn 7 in the final minutes of Q1.

Sainz initially qualified P17 for Sunday's 57-lap race, the first to be held at the Madring, while Bottas was left in P20 as neither progressed through to the second part of Qualifying.

The stewards heard from both Sainz and Bottas post-session, as well as looking at on-board videos and data before making their decision.

They noted that: "The team failed to inform the driver of Car 55 about Car 77 closing in on a flying lap and the driver did not take any action to make way for the incoming car.

It added: "The Stewards determine that Car 55 unnecessarily impeded Car 77", and handed Sainz a penalty for his home race.

"Not a very clean session, two or three issues that cost us probably there at the end, five-milliseconds to get through to Q2," said Sainz before the post-Qualifying penalty.

"A combination of just lacking a bit of performance on the straights. After looking at that lap, a couple of tenths.

"Then going very early for the last run and also impeding Valtteri, I just heard we impeded him without any notice from the pit wall.

"Not our cleanest session. Still did a pretty good lap but unfortunately not enough to make it through to Q2."

title: Hamilton reflects on missing pole for Spanish GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes himself and Ferrari have "got to work harder" in order to increase performance, having missed out on pole position for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix.

The Briton headed into Qualifying on the back foot after crashing head-on into the barrier at the final corner in Free Practice 3, eventually stopping his damaged car after calls from the team to pull over on the way back to the pits.

The missed track time earlier on Saturday didn't seem to hamper the seven-time World Champion, though, and Hamilton sat on provisional pole position after the first flying laps in the pivotal Q3 session.

But Hamilton slipped down to fourth in the final reckoning despite improving his time and finishing less than two tenths behind polesitter, Lando Norris.

"The only thing to say about FP3 is nothing. Qualifying was pretty decent," said Hamilton when asked to reflect on his day.

"Generally been feeling pretty decent. It takes everything for us to be able to compete with the two powerhouse motors [Mercedes and McLaren] ahead.

"They just seem to be able to turn the engine up or something when we get to Qualifying which we can't match. We've got to work harder."

Ferrari team mate Charles Leclerc finished directly behind Hamilton and was also within two tenths of Norris' top time, with the Monegasque believing he over-drove in the final segment of Qualifying.

"I think the lap was pretty good in Q3, it's a tricky Qualifying where you've got to go fully committed into Q3 and I did that," he said.

"But I felt like I maybe went over the limit a little in some corners and lost a little bit on top of maybe losing down the straights a bit because of running the older spec [engine].

"But at the end, that's on me. I think we did a good job today and we maximised our potential."

title: Norris ‘shocked’ by pole position in Madrid
excerpt:
Lando Norris admitted that he was “shocked” by his pole position in Qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix, with the Briton hailing the performance as “one of the best laps I’ve done ever in my career”.

The start of the weekend had not gone entirely smoothly for Norris, the World Champion having missed out on running during Friday’s second practice session following a gearbox issue on his car.

Things went better on Saturday, however, culminating in a surge to pole in Q3 with a lap time of 1m 31.824s, which put Norris 0.011s clear of championship leader Kimi Antonelli – a showing that even the man himself was not expecting.

“I’m shocked,” the McLaren driver said. “I’m a little bit surprised to be here now, but my god it was probably one of the best laps I’ve done ever in my career. Very, very happy, very proud, very happy for the team.

“It was just one of those laps where everything came together. I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, but it was whether my brain let me do it on the last lap and everything pretty much worked perfectly.

“I’m just very happy – one of those laps where you look at the lap time at the end and you’re like, ‘Oh, s*** that was pretty good’.”

Reflecting on the feeling of putting such a lap in around the new Madring circuit, Norris explained: “The adrenaline was high on the last lap. It’s just one where you’ve got to relax, just let it all flow.

“It’s easy to get tense around here, and there are a lot of walls that come at you pretty quickly. Honestly I’ve been feeling pretty confident and the car was feeling good, so I felt good out there.

“I just wasn’t doing what I wanted – I wasn’t quite relaxed, and on the last lap just took a good breath and everything kind of came together.

“It was pretty much perfect, bar the last corner – I thought I was in the wall, and I thought the boys were going to have to repair the car tonight. It could have been a little bit better, but nonetheless it was one of the best laps I’ve done.

“Just everything that I wanted to achieve I achieved, and that’s one of moments where you’re kind of in that flow state and it puts a big smile on my face, so I’m happy.”

When asked for his thoughts on Sunday’s race, Norris – who will line up ahead of Antonelli and Max Verstappen – joked: “I don't know, I'm still thinking about my lap!

“I've given myself the best chance for tomorrow. I don't think it's going to be the easiest track to overtake, but it's going to be possible and I've got two pretty quick, pretty good drivers behind me.

“I'm excited – the first race here in Madrid, it's been a pleasure so far. A lot of things can happen. It's a long race, a difficult track, so looking forward to the whole thing.”

title: ‘Hurts a lot’ – Bearman after crash rules him out of Qualifying
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman admits it "hurts a lot" after a crash in Free Practice 3 prevented the Haas driver from competing in Qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Briton was left as a bystander on Saturday afternoon at the Madring as the American team were unable to repair his damaged Haas in time for Qualifying.

Bearman lost control through the sweeping left of Turn 10 at Formula 1's newest venue in the dying seconds of the final practice session, before spinning and making heavy contact with the wall.

Although Bearman was left unharmed after the accident, just two hours remained before the start of Qualifying, with FP3 having also been delayed by 30 minutes due to barrier damage from Lewis Hamilton's earlier crash.

"It's a shame to be standing here right now," said Bearman as he performed media duties with Qualifying still underway.

"The car was quick. Yesterday was a tough day, but we made some changes overnight and the car was feeling really good in FP3.

"Unfortunately I got caught out in Turn 10 on that final lap – a combination of tyres were a bit older and I had a gust of wind not in my favour, so yeah, it's a shame.

"I shouldn't have made that mistake. It hurts a lot because the car is strong, but I'm sure that there can be some opportunities tomorrow."

It means Bearman will start at the back of the grid for Sunday's 57-lap race, with overtaking expected to be difficult around the narrow but high-speed circuit.

But new upgrades introduced in Monza last weekend, and team mate Esteban Ocon taking P13 on the grid in Spain, have given Bearman a glimmer of hope.

Bearman added: "We have to dust ourselves off and look at the positives, and the positive is that the car was fast and we'll be giving it everything to do the best we can tomorrow."

title: Norris denies Antonelli pole position for Spanish GP
excerpt:
Lando Norris charged to pole position for the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring with a spectacular last-gasp effort, beating Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen to the top spot.

In a remarkably close conclusion to Q3, the reigning World Champion displaced all of his rivals with a time of 1m 31.824s, mastering the brand-new circuit to clinch his 19th career pole position.

Lewis Hamilton had been the driver to provisionally take P1 after the first runs before he dropped to P4, leading Charles Leclerc and the second Mercedes of George Russell.

Oscar Piastri endured another frustrating deficit to his McLaren team mate as he finished in seventh place, with Liam Lawson, Franco Colapinto and Arvid Lindblad – who had suitably recovered from his earlier crash in FP2 – rounding out the top 10 qualifiers.

Despite featuring towards the front throughout the weekend, Audi failed to make it into Q3, with Nico Hulkenberg settling for P11 in front of his team mate Gabriel Bortoleto.

Just behind, Esteban Ocon beat his compatriot and last week’s polesitter Pierre Gasly to P13, followed by Racing Bulls’ Yuki Tsunoda and the lead Williams of Alex Albon.

It was a less than satisfactory day for the home crowd as Carlos Sainz and Fernando Alonso were both eliminated in the opening phase of Qualifying, with the former also set to be investigated for an impeding incident.

They finished the session just ahead of the Cadillac duo of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, who was the driver allegedly blocked by Sainz. Neither Ollie Bearman nor Lance Stroll made it onto the track as Haas were unable to repair the Briton’s car after his FP3 crash, while the Aston Martin driver was restricted to the garage thanks to a suspected water pressure issue.

AS IT HAPPENED

Q1 – Mercedes drivers shine as Spaniards eliminated

Even after three practice sessions at the Madring, plenty of unknowns remained heading into Qualifying, especially as three red flags over FP2 and FP3 – caused respectively by crashes for Lindblad, Hamilton and Bearman – disrupted the running.

The track action so far had also demonstrated that traffic could create a significant obstacle in Qualifying, with the drivers set to jostle for the best position throughout Q1. However, someone who wouldn’t have to deal with that was Bearman, as Haas confirmed that the damage sustained to his VF-26 earlier in the day was too great to fix before Qualifying.

With just 18 minutes on the clock – and the possibility of further incidents – the majority opted to get their banker laps in early on, and the Cadillac pair led a long queue of cars onto the circuit when the light at the end of the pit lane turned green.

Antonelli was the first of the frontrunners to tick that goal off, posting a time of 1m 33.566s on the soft compound to shoot into P1 ahead of Red Bull’s Verstappen, who had gone for the alternative option of medium tyres and found himself 0.178s down.

Building on their Free Practice performance, Audi continued to impress as Bortoleto settled into P3 on his opening run, which soon became P5 when Norris completed his lap and Lawson went even faster to top the timesheets.

It looked like Antonelli would come close to reclaiming the position on his second effort, but the Italian locked up and was forced to bail out in order to avoid the barrier. While Verstappen, Leclerc and Hamilton were the next to improve, no one could defeat Lawson’s benchmark.

Meanwhile, there was a shaky moment for Mercedes’ Russell as he kissed the barrier in a mirror image of the error that damaged Albon’s suspension in FP3, with the Briton instructing his team to check for any similar consequences.

His lap was nevertheless enough for P7, putting him in a strong spot to make Q2. Those who weren’t looking as safe leading into the final minutes were home favourite Alonso, the aforementioned Williams driver, Cadillac’s Perez and Bottas, and Bearman and Stroll, neither of whom had appeared in the session.

While Albon managed to escape the elimination zone and get ahead of his team mate, his P16-worthy lap meant that both Spaniards were knocked out of the first stage of Qualifying in their home event, much to the displeasure of their supporters. Sainz was also noted for impeding Bottas, which will be investigated later in the day.

Unhappy with his original run, Russell went again and was successful in setting the fastest time yet – a 1m 33.211s – to head Antonelli, followed by the Red Bull pair of Lawson and Verstappen.

Knocked out: Sainz, Alonso, Perez, Bottas, Bearman, Stroll

Q2 – Verstappen flies while Audi miss out

The remaining 16 contenders took a few minutes to reset before returning to the circuit for Q2, and it was once again Antonelli who delivered the initial time to beat with a time of 1m 32.603s.

But his hold on P1 didn’t last for long as Red Bull showed that their early pace wasn’t a one-off, with Verstappen edging out the standings leader by 0.046s while Lawson wound up fourth, keeping the team in the mix for a front row start as long as they progressed to Q3.

As the first flurry of laps came to an end, the only drivers who hadn’t set a lap were Alpine’s Gasly and Colapinto – the latter only just held onto a snap around La Monumental, which caused him to abandon the attempt and head back to the pits.

The pair finally emerged for the last four minutes to contend for a spot in the final segment of Qualifying, with many teams predicting that their starting position would be invaluable around the tight, twisty Madring. Bortoleto, Tsunoda, Ocon and Albon joined them in the drop zone at this stage.

After a series of improvements, including a notable one that saw Colapinto snatch P7, both Audis failed to make Q3, along with Ocon, a “sad” Gasly who complained about a lack of grip, Tsunoda and Albon. They missed out to Lindblad and Piastri, who both narrowly squeezed into the top 10 with identical lap times while Verstappen clung onto P1.

Knocked out: Hulkenberg, Bortoleto, Ocon, Gasly, Tsunoda, Albon

Q3 – Norris seizes pole with phenomenal final lap

With a short break out of the way, it was time for the big one. Everyone knew that the Madring had plenty of bite, so it was no surprise that they were eager to fly from the get-go just in case a second lap wasn’t possible.

Antonelli’s opening effort was enough for P1 until Hamilton crossed the line, well and truly bouncing back from his FP3 error to claim provisional pole with a blistering 1m 32.079s lap to get ahead of both Mercedes drivers.

After a clean first run for all 10, fourth-placed Leclerc led Verstappen, the McLarens of Norris and Piastri, Lawson, Colapinto and Lindblad – would anyone be able to dig deep, take the fight to Hamilton and seize pole position?

Maintaining his role as the first man to finish the lap, Antonelli soared back into first place and Hamilton was unable to improve a second time, but few had anticipated what ended up being a stunning lap by Norris that earned the Briton his third pole position of the season.

He referred to it as “one of my best” as he outpaced the Italian by just 0.011s, with Verstappen also finding time late on to secure P3 ahead of Hamilton and Leclerc.

Russell’s title challenge took yet another blow as he finished P6 from Piastri, Lawson, and the ‘best of the rest’ representatives Colapinto and Lindblad.

Key quote

"I’m shocked, I’m a little bit surprised to be here now, but my god it was probably one of the best laps I’ve done ever in my career," Norris said. "Very, very happy, very proud, very happy for the team. It was just one of those laps where everything came together. I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, but it was whether my brain let me do it on the last lap and everything pretty much worked perfectly. I’m just very happy – one of those laps where you look at the lap time at the end and you’re like, ‘Oh, s*** that was pretty good’."

title: F2: Miyata claims maiden victory in Madrid Sprint Race
excerpt:
Ritomo Miyata achieved his first ever victory in Formula 2 with a strong performance in the inaugural Madrid Sprint Race.

Starting from second, the Hitech driver took the lead on the run to Turn 1 and managed two Safety Car restarts well before going on to win by over two and a half seconds.

Emerson Fittipaldi had started from pole, but after losing out he put in a mature drive to finish second – giving him his maiden F2 podium.

The AIX Racing driver was forced to hold on to his position for the final few laps under pressure from Laurens van Hoepen, who settled for P3 in his TRIDENT.

Campos Racing’s Noel Leon finished fourth ahead of Rodin Motorsport’s Martinius Stenshorne.

Invicta Racing’s Rafael Camara and Rodin’s Alexander Dunne had a race-long battle, with the Ferrari Driver Academy member holding on for P6, as home favourite Mari Boya took the final point in eighth.

Dino Beganovic is set to start from pole position in Sunday’s Feature Race ahead of Dunne.

title: Antonelli fastest in Madrid FP3 as Hamilton and Bearman crash
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli finished fastest in Free Practice 3 from Charles Leclerc ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix, as the session was red flagged twice after crashes for Lewis Hamilton and Ollie Bearman.

The Mercedes driver continued his leading pace from FP2 on Friday by setting the best time in the final one-hour session on Saturday, which was disrupted by 30 minutes due to incidents.

Despite the need for teams and drivers to gather as much information as possible at the new venue ahead of a crucial Qualifying session later on Saturday, it took until five minutes had elapsed before any cars ventured out.

The leading contenders waited even longer in order to get the most representative running possible, including Lando Norris despite missing almost the entirety of FP2 as the Briton's McLaren suffered a gearbox issue.

The reigning World Champion aborted his first flying lap with the soft Pirelli tyre after cutting the chicane at Turn 5, while the Ferraris of Hamilton and Leclerc moved to the top of the times.

Home hero Carlos Sainz just avoided making head-on contact with the barrier at Turn 7, with Williams team mate Alex Albon having earlier glanced the wall on the exit of Turn 20 and breaking a rear track rod.

title: Stroll gets grid penalty for Spanish Grand Prix
excerpt:
Lance Stroll will take a grid penalty at the Spanish Grand Prix after Aston Martin opted to fit a range of new power unit components.

Stroll’s AMR26 is now running its fifth internal combustion engine, turbocharger and MGU-K, sixth energy store unit and seventh PU-ANC.

As per the regulations, the first time the allocation of any power unit element is exceeded, a 10-place grid penalty will be applied, with the second time this occurs (and so on) resulting in a five-place grid drop – all penalties at the same event applying in a cumulative manner.

In this case, the use of a sixth energy store and a fifth MGU-K each carries a five-place grid penalty, and the use of a fifth internal combustion engine, fifth turbocharger and seventh PU-ANC each carries a 10-place grid penalty. Therefore Stroll has been hit with a 40 place grid drop.

If a driver incurs a penalty exceeding 15 grid places, they will be required to start the race at the back of the field regardless.

There have been reliability concerns for Aston Martin at the Madring, with Stroll suffering a suspected water pressure issue to prevent him from setting a time in Qualifying.

During Friday, the Canadian also experienced a suspected battery issue towards the end of Free Practice 2.

Team mate Fernando Alonso also suffered a clutch problem in the day’s first practice hour, before resuming his programme in the second session.

title: Lewis Hamilton suffers sudden Ferrari realisation as pole slips through fingers
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has described his sudden realisation that his Ferrari was set to struggle during the crunch point at the end of Spanish Grand Prix qualifying.

After the first runs in Q3, Hamilton held provisional pole and was on course for his first P1 start in a grand prix since the 2023 Hungarian GP, 73 races ago.

However, on the second run, Hamilton only improved his time by less than a tenth of a second, opening the door for rivals to leapfrog him.

Lando Norris, Kimi Antonelli, and Max Verstappen all broke the 1:32 barrier, by dipping into the 1:31s to leave Hamilton fourth on the grid - the second time this season he has lost out on pole in Q3 after leading the first runs, following Hungary, to Norris.

Reflecting, Hamilton was pleased with the performance his SF-26 had shown, but explained how he knew he was in trouble at the end of the out-lap of his second run.

"Qualifying was generally pretty straightforward, with no real issues," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"I felt pretty awesome on Q3 run one, and then just didn't have any more grip or power.

"It was good execution from the team. I think they did a really good job, but unfortunately, I just didn't have the pace [at the end]."

Later, speaking to Sky Sports F1, Hamilton expanded on some of the issues he faced during his second lap.

"The second lap was just as good as the other one, because it was the same time pretty much," he said.

"I think I was half a tenth quicker or something like that, but for some reason, we went into that last lap, and as I came around the last corner, I had understeer.

"I was like: 'Hey, maybe these front tyres are not switched on", and it just turns out that I had more rear and more understeer through the lap."

The article continues below.

Hamilton looks ahead to Spanish GP

As for the race itself, Hamilton was upbeat about the circuit, but wary of the lack of overtaking opportunities.

"I have no idea. I mean, I haven't seen the other races, but was told it was very hard to overtake," he said.

"It is a pretty cool track to drive, some go-kart-esque elements with the kerbs, which is cool, really cool banking, so I think they did a really great job."

title: Max Verstappen heavily criticises new Madring F1 circuit: 'That's BS'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has launched a pointed criticism of Formula 1's new Madring circuit, dismissing the idea that space constraints excuse the lack of overtaking opportunities as "BS".

Verstappen will start from third on the grid for Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix after finishing 0.140s adrift of pole-sitter in McLaren's Lando Norris, with championship leader Andrea Antonelli splitting the pair in second in his Mercedes.

Although the circuit presented a challenge for the drivers in qualifying, there are concerns the race will be a sterile one given the lack of passing places around the 22-corner layout.

Speaking to the media after qualifying, including RacingNews365, Verstappen said: "I like the grip. They did a good job with the Tarmac, even though in some places it's a bit too bumpy already for a new track.

"The corners, you can't overtake. So, in some places, the braking zones, they need to learn that it should never be that you have to steer, that you have to combine under braking, because it doesn't allow any kind of overtaking.

"For sure, in terms of track design, I think it can be better. I also think input from drivers in the future on track design can also help a lot.

"I know they will always come back to you and say, 'Yeah, but the space'. But that's BS. There's always a way to find an overtaking opportunity around a track."

Verstappen feels Madring changes needed for the future

Verstappen at least felt the event overall to be "very cool", and the organisers had done "a great job" in that respect.

He added: "Also, how quickly they made the track available, the information that was shared for the simulator, so in that sense, it's very good.

"But if you want to have better racing and overtaking, there are a few corners that can be changed."

Asked how Sunday's race is likely to unfold from his grid slot, the Red Bull driver replied: "It will be tough. Let's say, best-case scenario, you're faster, but you can't pass.

"There are no corners where you can pass, so you need to rely on people degging very aggressively, so it's going to be tough.

"The long runs here have been very tough, a lot of deg for everyone, so that will probably be the key point tomorrow, but even with that, I still need to figure out a corner where to pass."

title: George Russell recounts 'annoying' moment which wrecked Spanish GP qualifying
excerpt:
George Russell has detailed the "annoying" mistake which wrecked his Spanish Grand Prix qualifying and left him sixth on the grid.

Russell, who now trails team-mate Kimi Antonelli by 66 points in the drivers' standings, will be on the third row of the Madrid grid for the first grand prix in the Spanish capital since 1981, with Antonelli poised to extend his lead having taken second.

Russell did hold third place after the first runs in Q3 but was dumped down to sixth after Lando Norris improved to pole, with Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc also leapfrogging the Briton.

Recounting what had happened, Russell revealed how a time-loss at Turn 11, just before La Monumental, had ended his bid to earn a fifth pole of the season.

"No, I don't think so," Russell began to media, including RacingNews365, when asked if the wall tap had had any lasting damage.

"Obviously, it was slightly concerning in the moment, but the car was fine. I went out and topped the session afterwards, and then felt in the mix thereafter.

"But just the last lap, I was about three-tenths up, and at Turn 11, the tyres couldn't take it.

"I lost all the lap time thereafter, and so that was annoying.

"It is a strange [track surface]; it is very high-grip, but the tyres are sliding quite a lot, so [the race] is going to be really interesting with the [tyre] degradation."

The article continues below.

Russell bemoans lack of overtaking opportunities

On a track where overtaking looks difficult, Russell detailed how the design just did not aid overtaking, and pointed to the roundabout at Turns 5 and 6.

"It is Jeddah-esque because of the high-speed corners, but there is also some Baku with some awkward braking zones," he said.

"Maybe one small frustration is the design has a lack of clear overtaking opportunities. On every track, at the end of the long straight, you need a clear opportunity to overtake.

"And the longest straight here goes into a tight roundabout section."

title: Kimi Antonelli offers 'very intense' explanation after Lando Norris 'snatched away' pole
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli labelled qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix "very intense" after Lando Norris 'snatched away' pole position from the Mercedes driver.

The young Italian came up just 11 milliseconds short of the reigning F1 drivers' champion at the Madring.

It looked like Antonelli had done enough, but with Norris one of the last drivers to take the chequered flag, he was denied in gut-wrenching fashion.

Despite missing out on top spot, it was a good grid-setting session for Antonelli, with his nearest championship rivals, Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes team-mate George Russell, only able to go fourth and sixth-quickest, respectively.

Track position will be critical in the 57-lap race, with overtaking opportunities hard to come by on the all-new 22-corner circuit in the Spanish capital.

"I thought it was a good lap, but then this guy [gesturing to Norris] just snatched it away," Antonelli said after hopping out of his W17. "So good job to them [McLaren].

"On my side, a very intense qualifying. Difficult to get the balance right with the track being so hot, but the lap was pretty clean."

Antonelli details 'quite tricky' experience

Reflecting on how challenging the conditions were, Antonelli was keen to turn his focus to the grand prix, as he looks to extend his advantage over Russell from the current 66-point margin.

"Obviously, it's not easy to put the things together on a track like this, which is quite tricky," the seven-time grand prix winner added.

"But overall, I think we did a good job, and now we'll try to see what we can do tomorrow."

title: Lando Norris reveals crash fear ahead of nailing best lap of his F1 career
excerpt:
Lando Norris has revealed he came within inches of ploughing his McLaren into a wall en route to securing a sensational pole for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Norris did not appear in the mix before his stunning final lap at the new Madring circuit, but somehow finished just 0.011s ahead of championship leader Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli.

"I'm shocked," said Norris. "I'm a little bit surprised to be here now. My God, it was probably one of the best laps I've done - ever in my career."

Over the radio a few minutes earlier, Norris had said that his lap "might be the best one".

Declaring himself "very happy, very proud, very happy for the team", he added: "It was one of those laps where everything came together.

"I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, but it was whether my brain would let me do it on the last lap, and everything pretty much worked perfectly.

"I'm just very happy. It's one of those laps where you look at the lap time at the end, and you're like, 'Oh shit! That was pretty good'."

[Article continues below]

Norris feared overnight repairs for McLaren mechanics

The lap handed Norris the 19th pole of his F1 career, and third this season, but he confirmed it almost never was.

"The adrenaline was high on the last lap," he said. "It's just one where you have to relax, let it all flow. It's easy to get tense around here, and there are a lot of walls that come at you pretty quickly.

"Honestly, I've been feeling pretty confident, and the car was feeling good, so I felt pretty good out there. I just wasn't doing what I wanted. I wasn't feeling relaxed. The last lap, I just took a good breath, and everything came together.

"It was pretty much perfect, but the last corner I thought I was in the wall, and the boys would have to repair the car tonight.

"So it could have been a little bit better, but nevertheless, it was one of the best laps I've done. Everything I wanted to achieve, I achieved. That's one of the moments where you're in that flow state, and it has put a big smile on my face, so I'm happy."

title: Lando Norris stuns Kimi Antonelli to steal sizzling Spanish GP pole
excerpt:
Lando Norris denied Kimi Antonelli at the very end to steal the Spanish Grand Prix pole position as George Russell's challenge fell away.

Lando Norris stunned Kimi Antonelli at the end of Spanish Grand Prix qualifying to steal pole position by just 0.011s.

Norris, who missed all of FP2 with a gearbox issue, placed only sixth after the first runs in Q3, with Lewis Hamilton holding provisional pole ahead of Antonelli and George Russell.

However, on his final flying lap, Norris posted a 1:31.824 lap, just 0.011s faster than Antonelli, who had taken provisional pole from Hamilton.

Hamilton himself found only 0.066s on his second flying lap and slipped to fourth as Max Verstappen nipped ahead.

It is Norris's third pole of the season, with Charles Leclerc in fifth, and George Russell down in sixth, having been third after the first Q3 runs.

Lando Norris stuns Kimi Antonelli to steal sizzling Spanish GP pole

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Hamilton and then Norris on pole

After the first runs in Q3, Hamilton's 1:32.079s was good enough to hold provisional pole from Antonelli on a 1:32.140 and Norris on a 1:32.525 down in sixth place.

Antonelli initially then found 0.244s to move up to provisional pole as Russell's challenge faltered, leaving the door open for Norris.

He found 0.701s on his second lap, which he labelled as "one of the best laps" of his career.

It was 0.011s faster than Antonelli, with Verstappen in third, ahead of Hamilton in fourth, who found only less than a tenth of improvement on his second run.

Leclerc was fifth, ahead of Russell with Oscar Piastri, Liam Lawson, Franco Colapinto, and Arvid Lindblad rounding out the top 10.

© XPBimages

Gasly fails to equal Monza heroics

The big story in Q2 was the elimination of Italian GP pole-sitter Pierre Gasly.

Gasly, who like team-mate Colapinto had just a single run at the end of the segment, could only place 14th, nearly seven-tenths slower than Colapinto, who was eighth.

Nico Hulkenberg led the Audi's, but dropped out by 0.019s as Lindblad got through, with Gabriel Bortoleto slotting in behind his team-mate.

Esteban Ocon was 13th ahead of Gasly in 14th, with Yuki Tsunoda and Alex Albon completing the eliminees in 15th and 16th.

Up front, Verstappen topped the segment from Antonelli and Hamilton.

© XPBimages

Double Spanish disappointment in Q1 in Madrid

Following his FP3 accident earlier in the day, Oliver Bearman was ruled out of qualifying, meaning just five cars were eliminated in Q1.

It was a double Spanish disappointment following the segment, as Carlos Sainz and Fernando Alonso were both eliminated.

Sainz fell just 0.005s from safety, dropping team-mate Albon into the drop-zone.

Both Cadillacs also fell, with Sergio Perez out-qualifying Valtteri Bottas once again, as Bearman and Lance Stroll failed to set a lap-time.

Stroll was set to start at the rear regardless, owing to power unit component changes.

Up front, Russell topped the segment from Antonelli and Lawson, as Verstappen, Hamilton, and Leclerc all got through by using the medium tyres.

excerpt:

title: Oliver Bearman ruled out of F1 qualifying after heavy FP3 shunt
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman will not take part in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix after his crash at the end of the final free practice session.

Haas was unable to sufficiently repair his car in time for the grid-setting session at the Madring, which means the British driver will start Sunday's race from the rear of the field.

The 21-year-old found the wall at Turn 11 with less than a minute of FP3 remaining, a session in which he finished P13, half a tenth adrift of team-mate Esteban Ocon.

Minutes before qualifying was due to get underway, the boards were up at the Haas driver's garage, and little work appeared to be happening on his car.

Just as the session got going, the American team confirmed the inevitable.

"Ollie Bearman will not participate in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix as a result of the damage sustained to his VF-26," the team said.

It is not yet clear what the extent of the repairs that will need to take place are, but if a chassis change has been required, Bearman would not have been able to take part in qualifying anyway, as the team would have to self-scutineer, and that process cannot be done between sessions.

title: McLaren pushing to accelerate Max Verstappen ally's Red Bull exit - report
excerpt:
McLaren is in talks with Red Bull to bring forward Gianpiero Lambiase's move to Woking, according to reports.

The development means Max Verstappen could be without his trusted race engineer for as many as three race weekends towards the tail end of the F1 season.

It was confirmed earlier this year that Lambiase will leave Red Bull for McLaren no later than 2028, where he will take on the role of chief racing officer under team principal Andrea Stella.

At Red Bull, Lambiase served as both head of racing and Verstappen's race engineer throughout the Dutchman's championship-winning years.

Tom Hart being readied as Verstappen's new engineer

From next season, Tom Hart will step in as Verstappen's permanent race engineer. Hart is already being prepared for the role, and RacingNews365 understands he will take full charge of three race weekends in 2026, understood to be Austin, Brazil and Las Vegas.

He was previously given his first outing alongside Verstappen during a practice session at Monza.

Beyond the Hart preparations, De Telegraaf reports that McLaren is actively pushing to shorten Lambiase's gardening leave period.

The team are said to be reluctant for him to sit at home for an entire year before joining, prompting Zak Brown to open discussions with Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies over an earlier start date.

The expectation now is that Lambiase will no longer be in Red Bull employment by 2027.

Red Bull have already moved to fill the void on the management side, recently confirming the signing of Tom McCullough as the new head of racing.

The Briton arrives from Aston Martin and slots directly into the role Lambiase vacated within the leadership structure around Mekies.

title: 2026 Spanish Grand Prix - F2 Madrid Sprint Race results
excerpt:
Ritomo Miyata claimed his first Formula 2 victory in a Spanish sprint which had huge effects on the title race.

The sole Hitech in the field after Colton Herta's withdrawal, Miyata eased to a breakthrough victory, but the biggest drama centred around championship leader Nikola Tsolov.

Tucked up behind Campos team-mate Noel Leon, Tsolov requested to be let through into fourth place to ease ahead of title rival Rafael Camara, who was running in sixth to earn more points than the Ferrari junior.

However, Campos did not issue the instruction, meaning Tsolov remained behind Leon until he clipped a wall in the final sector and stalled the car, leading to a DNF.

This then gave Camara a perfect opportunity to reduce the 11-point gap to Tsolov, which he did with a sixth-placed finish, earning three points, thus holding 169 points to Tsolov's 177, a deficit of eight.

Emerson Fittipaldi Jr and Laurens van Hoepen completed the Sprint podium.

title: Toto Wolff strikes back at 'couch warriors' with 'complete bullshit' defence
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has dismissed suggestions that George Russell was disadvantaged by Mercedes' decision to pit Kimi Antonelli under the virtual safety car at the Italian Grand Prix, calling the criticism from "couch warriors" as "complete bullshit".

Antonelli won at Monza from Russell, the pair finishing 3.8s apart to complete a Mercedes one-two at the championship leader's home race. It extended Antonelli's lead in the drivers' standings to 66 points over his team-mate, with Mercedes now 122 clear of Ferrari in the constructors' championship.

The flashpoint was the mid-race virtual safety car period, which allows a car to be pitted at a reduced time loss because track speeds fall while the pit lane limit stays the same. Mercedes brought in Antonelli, who had started on the hard tyre and switched to the medium.

Russell, already running hards, was in the lead from Antonelli and stayed out. Pirelli had gone into the weekend expecting a one-stop to be the likely route at Monza, with rear tyre temperatures the main thing to manage rather than outright degradation.

Asked whether Russell should have had priority in the call, the Mercedes team principal was blunt.

Discussing questions raised as to whether Russell should have had priority in the decision-making in Monza, Wolff replied to Sky F1: "No, it's absolutely the right thing we did.

"He was on the hards; it was predicted to be a one-stop as the better strategy. The medium was a compromise. We had to put the medium on Kimi because he started on the hards.

"There is just no way, and obviously there are some couch warriors that will drop their comments after having watched some other material online, saying that he [Russell] was penalised.

"It's complete bullshit. Sorry, I should say that it's complete crap."

Wolff wary of Spanish GP qualifying 'yo-yo' threat

Wolff was speaking after final practice in Madrid, where Antonelli again set the pace. The 20-year-old lapped the Circuito de Madring in 1m 32.797 to head Charles Leclerc by 0.166s, with Russell only sixth, 0.702s adrift.

Looking ahead to qualifying, Wolff said: "I think if we put it all together, we fight for pole and we fight for the first row.

"But it could be a little bit of yo-yoing. It could be all within a tenth. So you could be on the good side of it or on the wrong side."
